stages.name: The price mechanism
stages.title: The price mechanism
stages.sub: How rising and falling prices guide buyers and sellers in any market, from a local shop to the whole world.

steps.q: Onions are in short supply after a poor harvest, so buyers want more than farmers can offer at the old price. As the price rises and market forces work to close this gap, what happens to the size of the gap between what buyers want and what farmers offer?
steps.hint: You already know market forces eliminate excess demand and excess supply. What happens to that gap as price keeps adjusting?

steps.q: As the onion price rises and that gap closes, a farmer notices they can now earn much more per tonne than last year. What is the farmer likely to do?
steps.wrong: Grow the same amount as before
steps.hint: Think about what the higher price makes it worthwhile for the farmer to do.

steps.q: You walk past the greengrocer and see onion prices have doubled since last month. Even before anyone tells you, what does that price rise tell you about onions right now?
steps.wrong: They are more plentiful than before
steps.hint: You already know rationing shares out scarce onions by price. What does the price itself reveal about supply and demand conditions, without anyone explaining?

steps.q: A flood wipes out half the local cabbage crop in one town, prices there rise, and nearby farmers rush in extra supplies. Could the very same rationing, signalling and incentive effects also play out for oil traded between countries across the whole world?
steps.right: Yes, the same effects work at any scale
steps.wrong: No, they only work in small local markets
steps.hint: Does the size of the market change what a price rise tells buyers and sellers, or just how many of them there are?
